content:
For integer points \(P=(a,b)\), \(Q=(x,y)\), the segment \(PQ\) has no other integer points iff
\[
\gcd(|a-x|,\ |b-y|)=1.
\]

**Lower bound.** A single point \(Q=(x,y)\) cannot see all points of \(S\): choose \(P=(a,b)\in S\) with the same parity as \(Q\), i.e. \(a\equiv x\pmod 2\), \(b\equiv y\pmod 2\). Such a point exists and can be chosen distinct from \(Q\). Then both coordinate differences are even, so \(\gcd(|a-x|,|b-y|)\ge 2\). Thus one point is not enough, so \(|T|\ge 2\).

**Construction with 2 points.** Take
\[
T=\{(0,0),(1,0)\}.
\]
For \(P=(a,b)\in S\):
- If \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), then \(P\) is visible from \((0,0)\).
- If \(\gcd(a,b)>1\), the only possibilities in \(1\le a,b\le 5\) are
\[
(2,2),(2,4),(3,3),(4,2),(4,4),(5,5).
\]
For these, the differences from \((1,0)\) are
\[
(1,2),(1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(3,4),(4,5),
\]
all of which have gcd \(1\). So each such \(P\) is visible from \((1,0)\).

Therefore the minimum number of elements required in \(T\) is
\[
\boxed{2}.
\]
